Continued uncertainty surrounding shipping through the Kerch Strait and the Strait of Hormuz helped sustain a geopolitical risk premium across agricultural markets. July 23, 2026 By Fastmarket team Agriculture Grains and oilseeds Wheat Escalating disruptions to Black Sea grain logistics continued to support wheat prices, as port damage, vessel cancellations and export uncertainty in Russia and Ukraine increased the premium for reliable export origins. Additional support came from concerns over US spring wheat production after the first day of the annual North Dakota crop tour estimated average hard red spring wheat yields at 46.0 bushels per acre, 8% below last year’s result. Wheat prices was further bolstered by increasingly bullish fund positioning on Euronext, where the net long in milling wheat climbed to its highest level since June 2022 as investors added long positions and reduced short exposure. EU wheat exports Meanwhile, EU wheat exports totaled 0.47 million tonnes by July 19, down from 0.86 million tonnes during the same period a year earlier, indicating a slower start to the bloc’s export campaign. However, ongoing logistical disruptions in the Black Sea continued to support demand for alternative export origins and helped offset the competitive pressure from European supplies. The soft red winter (SRW) September futures contract on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange rose by 4.17%, or $0.28 per bu, day on day to $7.06 per bu. The Kansas hard red winter (HRW) September futures contract rose by 4.26%, or $0.31 per bu, to $7.64 per bu. The Minneapolis hard red spring September futures on MIAX Futures Exchange rose by $0.24 per bu to $7.29 per bu and the Euronext milling wheat September futures rose by €10.00 per tonne to €244.75 ($279.29) per tonne. Australian wheat export values weakened in the nearby August loading window on Wednesday, with both APW and ASW assessments moving lower amid limited buying interest and a softer prompt market structure. FOB Australia APW 10.5% wheat for August loading was assessed at $279 per tonne, down by $2 per tonne day on day, while September loading remained unchanged at $280 per tonne. Market participants reported subdued demand for prompt shipment positions, with bids heard below assessed values. Similarly, FOB Australia ASW 9.5% wheat for August loading was assessed at $275 per tonne, down by $2 per tonne, while September values were unchanged at $275 per tonne. The decline reflected weaker nearby market indications and a lack of aggressive importer demand. In the Black Sea, selling indications for Russian 12.5% wheat were reported going lower at $238-$240 per tonne FOB Novorossiysk-Taman-Tuapse (NTT) for August-September loading, with bids lower by $2 per tonne day on day at $233 per tonne for August. An alleged deal was reported at $235 per tonne FOB NTT for loading in September, but Fastmarkets could not confirm any further details on it. Russian 11.5% wheat was reported $1 higher day-on-day at $236 per tonne FOB NTT for loading in August. Offers for Ukranian 11.5% wheat were seen again at $230-$233 per tonne FOB Pivdennyi-Odesa-Chornomorsk (POC) for August-September loading. Black Sea region update In the EU Black Sea region, on the Constanta-Varna-Burgas (CVB) market, limited Ukrainian logistics capacity has not yet translated into significant price support. Market participants said the main source of support currently comes from OAIC demand, with traders holding large OAIC-related positions paying premiums. Outside of this, the market remains focused on finding demand rather than competing for limited logistics capacity. There was a lack of offers on an FOB Constanța basis for 12.5% protein wheat. According to some sources, protein quality can be an issue in Romania this year, while others suggested there may still be outstanding short positions from the Saudi tender, supporting demand for 12.5% protein wheat. Selling ideas for 11.5% wheat on an FOB CVB basis were reported at €10 per tonne below the September Euronext wheat contract for August, also some offers were seen at $265-$266 per tonne FOB CVB. Offers for feed wheat on an FOB CVB basis were seen at €15 per tonne below the September Euronext wheat contract for August. Trading activity across European wheat markets remained quiet on Wednesday, despite a stronger performance in futures. Matif wheat extended gains as broader agricultural markets drew support from another sharp rise in energy prices and a threatening US weather outlook, while ongoing disruptions to commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and Kerch Strait continued to underpin risk sentiment. In the physical market, activity remained limited. Sellers kept offers largely unchanged, showing little willingness to follow futures higher, while buying interest remained scarce, with bids largely absent from the market. Participants continued to monitor geopolitical developments and weather risks, but firm price ideas from both sides of the market left trading opportunities difficult to uncover. French 11% protein wheat was assessed at a premium of €2 per tonne to the September Euronext wheat contract for September loading. Polish 12.5% wheat cargo premiums were assessed at parity to the December Euronext wheat contract for September loading. Baltic FOB 12.5% wheat cargo premiums were assessed at a discount of €1 per tonne to the December Euronext wheat contract for September loading. The German 12.5% FOB wheat APM for September loading was assessed at €2 per tonne above the December Euronext contract due to a lack of fresh indications. No data was excluded. The German 11.5% FOB wheat APM for September loading was assessed at €2.50 per tonne below the December Euronext contract due to a lack of fresh indications. No data was excluded. US wheat cash markets US wheat cash markets moved higher on Wednesday, following the jump in futures markets as escalating attacks on infrastructure between Ukraine and Russia renewed concerns over Black Sea export flows. The heightened geopolitical tensions supported prices, with market participants closely monitoring the potential impact on grain exports from the region. The 11% FOB US Gulf HRW premiums were unchanged, with September at $1.50 per bu over the September Kansas HRW futures contract and October at $1.55 per bu over the December contract. The 10.5% FOB US Gulf SRW premiums were also unchanged, with September at 75 cents per bu over the September Chicago SRW futures contract and October at 85 cents per bu over the December contract. The 10% FOB Pacific Northwest soft white wheat market was higher, with September at $267 per tonne and October at $272 per tonne. Canadian western red spring 13.5% FOB Vancouver front-month premiums were unchanged, with September at 93 cents per bu over the September Minneapolis Grain Exchange (MGEX) futures and October at 85 cents per bu over the December contract. Canadian durum prices were steady, with 14.5% cargoes at $270 per tonne FOB Vancouver and $290 per tonne FOB St Lawrence. FOB Argentina wheat values were supported by broader gains in global wheat markets, as renewed Black Sea shipping risks, weaker US spring wheat conditions and crop downgrades in Russia and France reduced competitive pressure from key exporting origins. Higher Argentine new-crop wheat sales reflected improved market sentiment and favorable pricing conditions, while strong export commitments continued to underline demand for Argentina-origin material. For August, Argentina 11.5% wheat was assessed at $253 per tonne, and for September at $254 per tonne. Fastmarkets’ assessment for August and September increased both by $13 per tonne day on day. Fastmarkets’ assessment for feed barley FOB Argentina for August loading at Atlantic ports at $217 per tonne. New information was also disclosed for July, with offers at $225 per tonne and bids at $210 per tonne. Canada and EU forge closer ties – The Latest Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, has welcomed the EU’s proposal for Canada to become the bloc’s first ‘associate member’, despite threats from Donald Trump over the plan. The US president said Washington could impose ‘very serious tariffs’ or halt trade if the EU went ahead with the idea. But in a defiant speech to the European parliament, Carney called for ‘deep cooperation’ and said polling showed the overwhelming majority of Canadians supported closer ties with Europe.
